newsitem.title: UK: Major, facing defeat, plays British unity card.
newsitem.headline: Major, facing defeat, plays British unity card.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major went on a whirlwind tour of Britain on Monday in what looked increasingly like a doomed attempt to save his Conservative government from defeat in Thursday's election.

With all the signs pointing to an overwhelming victory for Tony Blair's new-look Labour Party, Major visited Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales to show his concern that a Blair government could bring about the dismantling of Britain.
Blair warned his party that it must not assume the victory for which it has been waiting since Margaret Thatcher swept to power in 1979 was assured.
"This election is not over until it is over. The only poll that counts is the election. I don't think this is a landslide country," he told a news conference.

Aides said he later penned a message to senior Labour MPs who may join his cabinet on Friday warning against complacency and reminding them Labour needs a 4.3 percent swing for outright victory, greater than any it has achieved since 1945.

Blair, who has led his party to the centre ground of politics in the three years of his leadership, jettisoning traditional tax-and-spend policies, is benefitting from deep divisions within the Conservatives, notably over Europe.
The latest poll gave Labour a 19-point lead over the Conservatives, barely changed from March 17 when Major announced a six-week election campaign -- the longest for 80 years.
Bookmakers William Hill cut the price on Labour winning the highest number of seat to 1/9, the shortest odds it has quoted for an election, with the Conservatives at 5/1.
If polls are right Labour could win the biggest majority in its history. London Evening Standard expert Peter Kellner said he expected a 121-seat majority in the 659-member House of Commons.
Blair will reinforce his no-complacency message on Tuesday with a visit to Gloucester, the marginal seat which Labour calculates it must win to get an overall majority.

The optimism of pro-Conservative newspapers which rejoiced at the one poll of the campaign to put the Conservatives within striking distance of Labour -- just five points behind -- has melted away. In its place is an increasing interest in a post-election battle for the party's leadership.
"Tories battle to halt election wipeout", said the Daily Mail. The headline of its rival, the Express, read: "Major's last bid to avert disaster".

In an interview with the Daily Telegraph, Major insisted that despite the polls, the atmosphere in the country was similar to that in 1992 when Britain's electors gave him a surprise 21-seat majority.
"There is no feeling of hostility, no great feeling for radical change," he said. "It doesn't have that feel about it at all -- and I have contested quite a few elections now."

Major's Northern Ireland visit, amid heavy security, underlined his determination not to allow the Irish Republican Army to disrupt polling day, despite recent bomb warnings which have brought chaos to British motorways and railways.
In Edinburgh, Scotland, Major claimed Labour's plans for constitutional change, and in particular for mini-parliaments for Scotland and Wales, could imperil the unity of Britain.
"Realise what is at stake," he told a crowd of about 200. "The history and future of Scotland and the rest of the United Kingdom...I mean that quite literally."

Blair accused the ruling party of "weakness, division and drift" and claimed that if it won a fifth consecutive term of office, Britain's National Health Service would be next in line for the privatising zeal that it has shown.
